expectedText:
REVOCABLE LIVING TRUST
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Alameda County

DECLARATION
I, Jordan Alex Lee, of Alameda County County, California, as settlor, declare that I am creating the The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust, and that I am transferring the property described in the attached schedule to Jordan Alex Lee, as initial trustee, to hold, administer, and distribute according to the terms of this trust. Upon the death, resignation, or incapacity of Jordan Alex Lee, Morgan Lee shall serve as successor trustee.

PERSONAL PROPERTY VS. REAL PROPERTY — DIFFERENT FORMALITY REQUIREMENTS
A trust of personal property carries no special formality requirement beyond what the law otherwise requires for the underlying transaction — an oral trust of personal property is legally possible, though its existence and terms can be established only by clear and convincing evidence, and the settlor's oral declaration alone is not enough. A trust relating to real property is held to a stricter standard: it isn't valid unless evidenced by a written instrument signed by the trustee (or the trustee's authorized agent), a written instrument conveying the property signed by the settlor (or the settlor's authorized agent), or by operation of law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A trust in relation to real property is not valid unless evidenced by one of the following methods: (a) By a written instrument signed by the trustee, or by the trustee's agent if authorized in writing to do so. (b) By a written instrument conveying the trust property signed by the settlor, or by the settlor's agent if authorized in writing to do so. (c) By operation of law."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15206 (California Legislative Information text), the written-instrument requirement for a trust of real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15206.)
  "(a) The existence and terms of an oral trust of personal property may be established only by clear and convincing evidence. (b) The oral declaration of the settlor, standing alone, is not sufficient evidence of the creation of a trust of personal property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15207(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), an oral trust of personal property is legally possible (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15207.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, easy-to-miss distinction — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This distinction matters beyond formality: a trust holds only the property actually transferred into it in a legally effective way, and real property that was never conveyed to the trustee by a qualifying written instrument remains outside the trust regardless of what the trust instrument says about it — meaning it stays subject to probate at the settlor's death rather than passing under the trust.

HOW A TRUST IS CREATED
California law recognizes several distinct methods of creating a trust: a declaration by the owner of property that the owner holds the property as trustee; a transfer of property by the owner, during the owner's lifetime, to another person as trustee; a transfer of property by will or other instrument taking effect at the owner's death; the exercise of a power of appointment in favor of a trustee; or an enforceable promise to create a trust. This trust is created by Jordan Alex Lee's lifetime transfer of property to Jordan Alex Lee as trustee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Subject to other provisions of this chapter, a trust may be created by any of the following methods: (a) A declaration by the owner of property that the owner holds the property as trustee. (b) A transfer of property by the owner during the owner's lifetime to another person as trustee. (c) A transfer of property by the owner, by will or by other instrument taking effect upon the death of the owner, to another person as trustee. (d) An exercise of a power of appointment to another person as trustee. (e) An enforceable promise to create a trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15200 (California Legislative Information text), the statutory methods of creating a trust (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15200.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual methods California recognizes for creating a trust — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. A declaration or transfer that satisfies one of these methods still has to satisfy the separate requirements for a valid trust — settlor intent, a legal purpose, and (except for a charitable trust) an ascertainable beneficiary — addressed elsewhere in this document. This is a single statutory section (§ 15200); no additional independent source was found for this.

REQUIREMENTS FOR A VALID TRUST
Beyond using one of the statutory methods of creation, a trust is valid only if Jordan Alex Lee properly manifests an intention to create a trust, the trust is created for a purpose that is not illegal or against public policy, and — unless the trust is a valid charitable trust — there is a beneficiary who is ascertainable with reasonable certainty, or sufficiently described that it can be determined whether a given person meets the description, or whose selection is left to the trustee's or another person's discretion under a stated standard.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A trust is created only if the settlor properly manifests an intention to create a trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15201 (California Legislative Information text), the settlor's-intent requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15201.)
  "A trust may be created for any purpose that is not illegal or against public policy."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15203 (California Legislative Information text), the lawful-purpose requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15203.)
  "(a) A trust, other than a charitable trust, is created only if there is a beneficiary. (b) The requirement of subdivision (a) is satisfied if the trust instrument provides for either of the following: (1) A beneficiary or class of beneficiaries that is ascertainable with reasonable certainty or that is sufficiently described so it can be determined that some person meets the description or is within the class. (2) A grant of a power to the trustee or some other person to select the beneficiaries based on a standard or in the discretion of the trustee or other person."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15205 (California Legislative Information text), the ascertainable-beneficiary requirement and charitable-trust exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15205.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual requirements for a valid trust — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. These three requirements — intent, lawful purpose, and an ascertainable beneficiary — are independent of the funding requirements addressed elsewhere in this document; a trust can satisfy all three and still fail to hold property that was never actually transferred into it.

CONSIDERATION IS NOT REQUIRED
Unlike a contract, a trust does not require consideration to be valid — Jordan Alex Lee can create a trust as a gift, with nothing given in exchange. A promise to create a trust in the future is treated differently: that promise is enforceable only if it independently satisfies the requirements for an enforceable contract, consideration included.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Consideration is not required to create a trust, but a promise to create a trust in the future is enforceable only if the requirements for an enforceable contract are satisfied."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15208 (California Legislative Information text), consideration is not required to create a trust (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15208.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, easy-to-miss statutory rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is a single statutory section (§ 15208); no additional independent source was found for this.

REVOCABILITY — THE DEFAULT RULE AND HOW TO REVOKE
Unless The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust is expressly made irrevocable by its own terms, it is revocable by Jordan Alex Lee — revocability, not irrevocability, is the default under California law for a trust the settlor creates while domiciled in California, executed in California, or that states California law governs. Jordan Alex Lee can revoke the trust, in whole or in part, by following any revocation method the trust instrument itself provides, or — if the trust instrument doesn't make its own method the exclusive one — by a signed writing, other than a will, delivered to Jordan Alex Lee during Jordan Alex Lee's lifetime.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless a trust is expressly made irrevocable by the trust instrument, the trust is revocable by the settlor. This section applies only where the settlor is domiciled in this state when the trust is created, where the trust instrument is executed in this state, or where the trust instrument provides that the law of this state governs the trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15400 (California Legislative Information text), revocability is the statutory default (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15400.)
  "(a) A trust that is revocable by the settlor or any other person may be revoked in whole or in part by any of the following methods: (1) By compliance with any method of revocation provided in the trust instrument. (2) By a writing, other than a will, signed by the settlor or any other person holding the power of revocation and delivered to the trustee during the lifetime of the settlor or the person holding the power of revocation. If the trust instrument explicitly makes the method of revocation provided in the trust instrument the exclusive method of revocation, the trust may not be revoked pursuant to this paragraph."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15401(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory methods of revocation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15401.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default rule and revocation methods — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. Where more than one person contributed property to the same trust, or where someone other than the settlor holds a power of revocation, additional statutory provisions address revocation of just that person's contributed share; those situations aren't addressed here.

TRUSTEE'S DUTY OF LOYALTY AND DUTY TO KEEP TRUST PROPERTY SEPARATE
Jordan Alex Lee, acting as trustee, has a duty to administer the trust solely in the interest of the beneficiaries, and a separate duty to keep trust property separate from Jordan Alex Lee's own property and to see that trust property is identified as property of the trust.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) The trustee has a duty to administer the trust solely in the interest of the beneficiaries."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16002(a) (California Legislative Information text), the trustee's duty of loyalty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16002.)
  "The trustee has a duty to do the following: (a) To keep the trust property separate from other property not subject to the trust. (b) To see that the trust property is designated as property of the trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16009 (California Legislative Information text), the trustee's duty to keep trust property separate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16009.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of two genuine, specific fiduciary duties among several a trustee owes — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a complete list of a trustee's duties. A trustee who also administers a second trust may sell or exchange property between the two trusts without violating the duty of loyalty if the exchange is fair to both trusts' beneficiaries and both sets of beneficiaries are notified of the material facts — a narrow statutory exception to the general rule stated above.

WHOSE INTERESTS THE TRUSTEE SERVES WHILE THE TRUST IS REVOCABLE
For as long as the trust remains revocable and Jordan Alex Lee (or whoever else holds the power to revoke) is competent, the rights the law otherwise gives to trust beneficiaries belong instead to the person holding the power to revoke, and the trustee's duties run to that person — not to the beneficiaries named in the trust. Where a beneficiary's consent would otherwise be required or permitted for some action, it's the person holding the power to revoke, not the beneficiary, who has the power to give or withhold that consent, during that same period.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Except to the extent that the trust instrument otherwise provides or where the joint action of the settlor and all beneficiaries is required, during the time that a trust is revocable and at least one person holding the power to revoke the trust, in whole or in part, is competent, the following shall apply: (1) The person holding the power to revoke, and not the beneficiary, has the rights afforded beneficiaries under this division. (2) The duties of the trustee are owed to the person holding the power to revoke."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15800(a) (California Legislative Information text), trustee's duties run to the person holding the power to revoke (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15800.)
  "(a) In any case where the consent of a beneficiary may be given or is required to be given before an action may be taken, during the time that a trust is revocable and the person holding the power to revoke the trust is competent, the person holding the power to revoke, and not the beneficiary, has the power to consent or withhold consent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15801(a) (California Legislative Information text), consent rights belong to the person holding the power to revoke (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15801.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuinely counter-intuitive default — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. If, while the trust is still revocable, no one holding the power to revoke remains competent, the statute shifts the trustee's accounting and disclosure duties to the beneficiaries who would receive income or principal if the settlor had died at that point — the rule addressed in this clause is specifically about the period when someone with the power to revoke is still competent.

TRUSTEE'S DUTY TO ACCOUNT — AND ITS LIMITS WHILE THE TRUST IS REVOCABLE
Jordan Alex Lee, acting as trustee, has a duty to account at least annually, at the trust's termination, and upon any change of trustee, to each beneficiary currently entitled — or authorized in the trustee's discretion — to receive income or principal. That duty doesn't run to beneficiaries generally while the trust is revocable and someone holding the power to revoke remains competent — during that period, as stated elsewhere in this document, the accounting duty runs to the person holding the power to revoke instead.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in Section 16064, the trustee shall account at least annually, at the termination of the trust, and upon a change of trustee, to each beneficiary to whom income or principal is required or authorized in the trustee's discretion to be currently distributed."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16062(a) (California Legislative Information text), the trustee's duty to account (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16062.)
  "(a) The trustee is not required to account to the beneficiary, provide the terms of the trust to a beneficiary, or provide requested information to the beneficiary pursuant to Section 16061, in any of the following circumstances: (1) In the case of a beneficiary of a revocable trust, as provided in subdivision (a) of Section 15800, for the period when the trust may be revoked."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16069(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the accounting duty doesn't run to beneficiaries while the trust is revocable (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16069.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the accounting duty and how the statute itself reconciles it with the revocable-trust settlor's-interest rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. Additional statutory exceptions to the accounting duty exist beyond the revocable-trust exception addressed here, including a trust instrument's waiver of accounting (subject to its own limits) and a beneficiary's individual written waiver.

FILLING A VACANCY IN THE OFFICE OF TRUSTEE
If The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust has no trustee — including because Jordan Alex Lee has died or become incapacitated — the vacancy is filled first by whatever practical method or named successor the trust instrument itself provides. Only if the trust instrument doesn't fill the vacancy that way does the law step in: a trust company that agrees to accept the trust may fill the vacancy with the agreement of all adult beneficiaries currently entitled to income or principal, or a court may appoint a trustee on petition of an interested person or a person named as trustee in the trust instrument.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) If the trust instrument provides a practical method of appointing a trustee or names the person to fill the vacancy, the vacancy shall be filled as provided in the trust instrument. (c) If the vacancy in the office of trustee is not filled as provided in subdivision (b), the vacancy may be filled by a trust company that has agreed to accept the trust on agreement of all adult beneficiaries who are receiving or are entitled to receive income under the trust or to receive a distribution of principal if the trust were terminated at the time the agreement is made. If a beneficiary has a conservator, the conservator may agree to the successor trustee on behalf of the conservatee without obtaining court approval. Without limiting the power of the beneficiary to agree to the successor trustee, if the beneficiary has designated an attorney in fact who has the power under the power of attorney to agree to the successor trustee, the attorney in fact may agree to the successor trustee. (d) If the vacancy in the office of trustee is not filled as provided in subdivision (b) or (c), on petition of any interested person or any person named as trustee in the trust instrument, the court may, in its discretion, appoint a trustee to fill the vacancy."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15660(b)-(d) (California Legislative Information text), filling a vacancy in the office of trustee (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15660.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the statutory fallback for filling a vacant trusteeship — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is the mechanism a revocable living trust relies on to keep the trust administered without a court-supervised conservatorship if the settlor becomes incapacitated or dies — but it works automatically only if the trust instrument's own successor-trustee provision is functional; where it fails or is silent, the statutory fallback above requires either beneficiary agreement or a court petition, neither of which is automatic. This is a single statutory section (§ 15660); no additional independent source was found for this.

DISTRIBUTION ON DEATH
Upon my death, the trustee then serving shall distribute the trust property remaining after payment of my debts, expenses, and applicable taxes as follows: ☐ _________________________, with the remainder distributed to Jordan Alex Lee's children, in equal shares.

RELATIONSHIP TO A POUR-OVER WILL
California law allows a will to devise property to the trustee of a trust that the testator established, or is establishing, elsewhere — a trust identified in the will, with its terms set out in a written instrument other than the will itself, executed before, at the same time as, or within 60 days after the will. Property devised this way isn't treated as held under a separate trust created by the will; it simply becomes part of the trust it's given to, administered under that trust's own terms, and the devise isn't invalidated merely because the trust is amendable or revocable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) A devise, the validity of which is determinable by the law of this state, may be made by a will to the trustee of a trust established or to be established by the testator, by the testator and some other person, or by some other person (including a funded or unfunded life insurance trust, although the settlor has reserved any or all rights of ownership of the insurance contracts) if the trust is identified in the testator's will and its terms are set forth in a written instrument (other than a will) executed before, concurrently with, or within 60 days after the execution of the testator's will or in the valid last will of a person who has predeceased the testator (regardless of the existence, size, or character of the trust property). The devise is not invalid because the trust is amendable or revocable, or both, or because the trust was amended after the execution of the will or after the death of the testator. (b) Unless the testator's will provides otherwise, the property so devised (1) is not deemed to be held under a testamentary trust of the testator but becomes a part of the trust to which it is given and (2) shall be administered and disposed of in accordance with the provisions of the instrument or will setting forth the terms of the trust, including any amendments thereto made before or after the death of the testator (regardless of whether made before or after the execution of the testator's will)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6300(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), a will may devise property to a trustee (the pour-over statute) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6300.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory basis for a pour-over provision — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust or will. This is the mechanism connecting a companion will to a living trust: property the settlor never transferred into the trust during life, but that the will directs to the trust at death, still has to pass through probate to get there — a pour-over provision routes probate property into the trust rather than avoiding probate for that property. If the trust is revoked or terminated before the testator's death, the devise lapses unless the will itself says otherwise. This is a single statutory section (§ 6300); no additional independent source was found for this.

SIGNATURE AND NOTARIZATION
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, Jordan Alex Lee, as settlor, and Jordan Alex Lee, as trustee, have signed this trust instrument on the date written below.

_________________________ Date: _________________________
Jordan Alex Lee, Settlor

_________________________ Date: _________________________
Jordan Alex Lee, Trustee

A notary public or other officer completing a notarial certificate for this instrument verifies only the identity of the individual who signed the document, not the truthfulness, accuracy, or validity of that document.

California law allows a will to devise property to the trustee of a trust that the testator established, or is establishing, elsewhere — a trust identified in the will, with its terms set out in a written instrument other than the will itself, executed before, at the same time as, or within 60 days after the will. Property devised this way isn't treated as held under a separate trust created by the will; it simply becomes part of the trust it's given to, administered under that trust's own terms, and the devise isn't invalidated merely because the trust is amendable or revocable.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6300(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a will may devise property to a trustee (the pour-over statute)
citations.quote: (a) A devise, the validity of which is determinable by the law of this state, may be made by a will to the trustee of a trust established or to be established by the testator, by the testator and some other person, or by some other person (including a funded or unfunded life insurance trust, although the settlor has reserved any or all rights of ownership of the insurance contracts) if the trust is identified in the testator's will and its terms are set forth in a written instrument (other than a will) executed before, concurrently with, or within 60 days after the execution of the testator's will or in the valid last will of a person who has predeceased the testator (regardless of the existence, size, or character of the trust property). The devise is not invalid because the trust is amendable or revocable, or both, or because the trust was amended after the execution of the will or after the death of the testator. (b) Unless the testator's will provides otherwise, the property so devised (1) is not deemed to be held under a testamentary trust of the testator but becomes a part of the trust to which it is given and (2) shall be administered and disposed of in accordance with the provisions of the instrument or will setting forth the terms of the trust, including any amendments thereto made before or after the death of the testator (regardless of whether made before or after the execution of the testator's will).

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory basis for a pour-over provision — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust or will. This is the mechanism connecting a companion will to a living trust: property the settlor never transferred into the trust during life, but that the will directs to the trust at death, still has to pass through probate to get there — a pour-over provision routes probate property into the trust rather than avoiding probate for that property. If the trust is revoked or terminated before the testator's death, the devise lapses unless the will itself says otherwise. This is a single statutory section (§ 6300); no additional independent source was found for this.
